title: US Approves $4.5B KC-46A Tanker Sale to Qatar as AeroVironment Plants Loitering-Munition Production in Greece
subhead: Washington cleared a four-aircraft Boeing tanker package for Doha while AeroVironment took a majority stake in a Greek joint venture to build drones and loitering munitions in Europe. Poland separately unveiled plans for 1,000km-range strike missiles on its eastern border.

sections.heading: US Clears $4.5B KC-46A Tanker Sale to Qatar
sections.body:
The US State Department on August 20 approved a $4.5 billion Foreign Military Sale of four Boeing KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling aircraft to Qatar, according to the congressional notification. The package includes eight Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines, radar warning receivers, missile-warning sensors, secure communications and logistics support, with Boeing, Pratt & Whitney, RTX and Northrop Grumman as principal contractors.

The deal would give the Qatar Emiri Air Force its own tanker capability for a combat fleet that already mixes Boeing F-15QAs, Dassault Rafales and Eurofighter Typhoons. The KC-46A refuels via both fly-by-wire boom and hose-and-drogue, covering the F-15QA's boom requirement and the Rafale and Typhoon's probe systems. Qatar previously considered the Airbus A330 MRTT but never ordered it.
sections.whyItMatters: Qatar is buying independent aerial-refueling reach rather than relying on allied tankers, a sign Gulf states are deepening self-sufficient air-power logistics even as the US-Iran pause holds. The sale still faces congressional review and is not a signed contract.

sections.heading: AeroVironment Takes Majority Stake in Greek Drone Venture
sections.body:
AeroVironment announced on August 20 it will establish an industrial presence in Greece through AV Eagle, a majority-owned joint venture with Athens-based Eyeonix SA, to manufacture and assemble unmanned aerial systems, loitering munitions and counter-drone systems for European defense and civil-protection customers. The venture has completed a shareholders agreement and secured Foreign Direct Investment approval from the Greek foreign ministry, with production capabilities expected by 2028.

The move is AeroVironment's fourth European localization step in roughly 18 months, following a Danish framework agreement, a partnership with UAS Denmark, and a UK co-production deal with TIA Group. It comes on a balance sheet reshaped by the BlueHalo acquisition: the company reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.98 billion, up 141% year-over-year, with its Autonomous Systems segment — home to the Switchblade loitering-munition line — generating $1.3 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: AeroVironment is shifting from exporting drones to building them inside Europe, betting on EU defense-industrial financing and doctrine. The Greek facility, tied to the Hellenic Center for Defence Innovation, positions loitering munitions and counter-drone systems as a core European procurement category.

sections.heading: US Military to Run Directed Energy 'Shoot-Off' in Counter-Drone Push
sections.body:
Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Pentagon's specialized counter-drone team, is running a directed energy pilot on five military installations — Fort Huachuca, Fort Bliss, Naval Base Kitsap, Grand Forks AFB and Whiteman AFB — and will hold a 'directed energy shoot-off' in December at Yuma Proving Ground, Brig. Gen. Matt Ross told DefenseScoop. The event, run with the Pentagon's research and engineering office, will pit commercial high-energy laser and high-power microwave systems against each other, with successful performers eligible for immediate purchase orders to start production lines.

Ross said the science of defeating drones with lasers and microwaves is proven, but the task force needs to learn how to operate them on bases without disrupting missions. The pilot places systems with actual service members for a 365-day period to gather data on power requirements, cost, repair tempo and tactics.
sections.whyItMatters: The shoot-off is a concrete step toward operationalizing directed energy for counter-drone defense, and the purchase-order incentive is designed to pull new commercial entrants into the market. It signals the Pentagon is moving from testing lasers to buying them at scale.

sections.heading: Poland Plans 1,000km-Range Strike Missiles on Eastern Border
sections.body:
Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said Warsaw will develop an 'East Sword' long-range strike capability under the 'East Shield' program, deploying missiles with a range of over 1,000 km along the eastern border, TASS reported. He cited JASSM cruise missiles (up to 370 km) and JASSM-ER (up to 900 km) as candidates, with plans to acquire weapons able to hit targets beyond 1,000 km.

On fortification, Poland has built 150 km of 'East Shield' defenses and plans another 50 km by year-end, plus 300,000 concrete anti-tank obstacles along the borders with Russia and Belarus by mid-October. The program is budgeted at about 10 billion zlotys ($2.5 billion) with completion targeted for 2028.
sections.whyItMatters: Poland is pairing physical fortification with long-range precision strike, a shift from purely defensive border hardening toward offensive deterrence. The 1,000km-plus requirement points to a capability that can reach deep into Russian territory from Polish soil.

sections.heading: Indonesia and China Agree to Build Ammunition Factory
sections.body:
Indonesia will build a China-backed ammunition factory with technology transfer, Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin said after a '2+2' meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Defense Minister Dong Jun in Jakarta on August 21. The cooperation covers missiles and rockets, with state firm Pindad joining the joint venture and electronics maker Len Industri handling electrical systems. Sjafrie said there were 'no talks' about Indonesia buying Chengdu J-10 fighters, contrary to earlier expectations.

The deal comes as Jakarta's military modernization accelerates under President Prabowo Subianto, including a contract for 48 Turkish-made KAAN fighters. China accounted for about 5.6% of global arms exports from 2021 to 2025, per Jakarta Globe, placing it fifth behind Germany.
sections.whyItMatters: The ammunition factory gives China a manufacturing foothold in Southeast Asia's largest defense market without a headline fighter sale. It reflects Jakarta's hedging — buying Western and Turkish platforms while accepting Chinese production and technology-transfer for munitions.

sections.heading: Russia's Zanoza FPV Drone Deliveries Top 11,000
sections.body: Russian manufacturer Zanoza Drones said it has delivered more than 11,000 Zanoza FPV drones to the war in Ukraine since 2022, including over 1,000 fiber-optic-controlled versions, TASS reported. The 10-inch Zanoza-10 carries a warhead of up to 3.5 kg over a confirmed strike range of 42 km, and the fiber-optic variant — immune to electronic jamming — uses 15-, 20- and 25-km cables. The company said it is working to extend fiber-optic range while maintaining signal reliability.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of Russian FPV production — 11,000 delivered with fiber-optic variants that defeat EW — shows Moscow has industrialized drone output and is pushing into jamming-immune designs, a direct counter to Ukraine's electronic-warfare advantage.

sections.heading: India's Cochin Shipyard Delivers Third ASW Craft
sections.body: Cochin Shipyard Limited handed over INS Mangrol, the third of eight Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft, to the Indian Navy, per Ocean News and Indian outlets. The indigenous vessel is designed to hunt submarines in shallow coastal waters, part of India's push to build ASW capability domestically rather than import it.
sections.whyItMatters: The delivery advances India's indigenous naval shipbuilding program, adding shallow-water ASW coverage along its coastline as New Delhi expands its maritime deterrent posture.

bottomLine: Today's defense news was dominated by procurement and industrial capacity rather than battlefield moves. Washington cleared a $4.5B tanker sale to Qatar and AeroVironment committed to building loitering munitions in Greece, while Poland unveiled a 1,000km-range strike plan and Indonesia accepted a Chinese ammunition factory. The common thread is localization: buyers from the Gulf to Southeast Asia and Europe are pushing for domestic production and technology transfer, and suppliers are responding by building factories rather than just shipping weapons.
sources: AeroTime, DefenseScoop, TASS, Jakarta Globe, Securities.io, Ocean News, Yahoo Finance
